   - **Regime characterization**: Type A (SC≥60%, confirmation bias), Type B (domain not formalizable), Type C (SC≤40%, noise), intermediate-SC region (~50-56% SC)

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluated Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA) across six models spanning three architecture families across three reasoning domains (FOLIO, ProofWriter, LogiQA), and over 3,000 evaluation instances with four-seed replication on the primary condition. Grounded in the Condorcet Jury Theorem, our analysis explains why Self-Consistency majority voting saturates and why symbolic constraint aggregation fails to break this plateau under same-model self-extraction.

The central finding is the independence bottleneck. Same-model traces produce Fleiss' $\kappa$ values of $0.21$--$0.82$ among instruction-tuned models (0.91 for thinking mode), and the effective sample size compresses to Eff-$K = 1.20$--$3.62$ at $K = 12$. Self-extracted FOL constraints inherit this correlation structure. We observe an intermediate-SC region around 50--55\% accuracy in one model-dataset condition (Mistral-7B on FOLIO): Mistral-7B on FOLIO shows a positive directional trend of $+3.43$\,pp ($p = 0.092$, 2 of 4 seeds marginal at $p < 0.10$, none reaching $p < 0.05$; 4-seed mean $+1.47$\,pp). Outside this zone, confirmation bias renders constraints non-discriminative (Type~A) or error amplification actively degrades accuracy by $-2.83$\,pp (Type~C).

Oracle controls confirm that the aggregation mechanism is sound: gold FOL annotations yield $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter (both $p < 0.001$), yet self-extraction captures only 24\% of this ceiling. Nine remediation strategies spanning six intervention dimensions all fail to widen the effective zone. The uniform failure confirms the bottleneck is structural rather than an engineering artifact. Sensitivity analysis reinforces this conclusion: $K = 12$ is the only setting with $\Delta > 2$\,pp among five $K$ values, and only 1 of 4 temperature settings ($T = 0.7$) produces a positive effect; both peaks coincide with a relatively low SC baseline.

The multi-candidate rate $C_0$ combined with SC accuracy provides a zero-cost deployment diagnostic for predicting when symbolic aggregation can help. Three paths forward trade simplicity for independence as CJT requires: trained extractors, external provers, and multi-model pipelines.

\paragraph{Limitations.} Our evaluation covers same-model self-extraction and cross-model extraction in both directions (\S\ref{sec:remediation}), but we do not test trained FOL extractors or external solvers with verified grounding, which may overcome the independence bottleneck. The intermediate-SC region where positive trends occur is narrow (SC $\approx$ 50--55\%) and observed in only one model-dataset condition, limiting practical applicability. The optimal $K$ and temperature settings cannot be determined without labeled data, as both sensitivity analyses show the best configuration coincides with the lowest SC baseline rather than following a predictable trend. Our evaluation covers formal reasoning benchmarks (FOLIO, ProofWriter, LogiQA) but lacks open-domain validation where formalizability is lower and failure modes may differ. Finally, four-seed replication on the primary condition (Mistral-7B on FOLIO) shows effects ranging from $+3.43$ to $-0.49$\,pp, with 2 of 4 seeds yielding null or negative results, indicating that even the most promising condition produces unreliable improvements.

Several limitations bound the scope of our conclusions. First, the oracle experiments cover two formal logic benchmarks (FOLIO $n = 204$, ProofWriter $n = 600$) that provide gold annotations; extending this analysis to commonsense or science domains requires constructing comparable gold constraint sets for those domains. Second, seven of our eleven model-domain conditions have $n \leq 60$, providing insufficient statistical power for confirmatory claims; power analysis shows that the minimum detectable effect exceeds 5\,pp for these conditions (Appendix Table~\ref{tab:power}), so they serve as regime characterization rather than definitive tests. Third, although we test cross-model constraint extraction in both directions (weaker extracting from stronger traces and vice versa, \S\ref{sec:remediation}), we do not compare against trained FOL extractors; whether models fine-tuned for logical formalization would produce more discriminative constraints remains untested. Fourth, all models tested range from 7B to 32B parameters; whether the capability trap persists at larger scales (70B+) remains an open question. Fifth, our extraction prompts use a single zero-shot template per domain; alternative prompting strategies (few-shot exemplars, chain-of-thought extraction, or iterative refinement) might yield higher-quality constraints, though the oracle gap suggests the bottleneck is fundamental rather than prompt-specific. Sixth, the constraint quality analysis (91.8\% Z3 semantic discriminative rate, 8.2\% non-discriminative rate, 39.2\% source-trace minority weight) covers Qwen2.5-14B on the full FOLIO + ProofWriter dataset ($N = 804$); other model-domain combinations may exhibit different constraint characteristics. Seventh, constraint extraction uses $T_{\text{ext}} = 0.3$ while trace sampling uses $T = 0.7$; alternative extraction temperatures might yield different constraint characteristics, though our negative results suggest the bottleneck is semantic coupling rather than extraction diversity. Eighth, StrategyQA and ARC-Challenge use the mathematical extraction prompt rather than the logical one because their reasoning structure does not involve formal predicates or implications (Appendix~\ref{app:prompts}); a domain-specific commonsense extraction template might yield different constraint characteristics for these benchmarks. Ninth, although we prompt for FOL-style formalizations, the extracted constraints are predominantly propositional ground clauses without quantifiers (\S\ref{sec:constraint-extraction}); whether models capable of producing genuine quantified FOL would yield higher discriminative rates is untested. Tenth, deduplication uses syntactic equivalence, so semantically equivalent constraints with different surface forms receive separate weights, potentially inflating the apparent constraint pool without adding discriminative content. Eleventh, the GSM8K pilot ($n = 30$) is included to illustrate the constraint-absent failure regime and should not be interpreted as confirmatory evidence.

Section~\ref{sec:failure-modes} attributes this to domain formalizability.
65	
66	\paragraph{Type A (SC $\geq$ $\sim$60\%): confirmation bias.} Nine conditions with SC $\geq 63\%$ (combined $N > 2{,}800$) produce no significant positive effects. Most yield $|\Delta| \leq 2.45$\,pp (nonsignificant), but LLaMA-3.1-8B on FOLIO shows $\Delta = -4.41$\,pp ($p = 0.093$, marginal) and Qwen2.5-14B on ProofWriter ($n = 600$, SC $= 75.17\%$) shows a significant negative effect: $\Delta = -2.50$\,pp ($p = 0.011$), indicating that symbolic aggregation can hurt even when the model is accurate. Qwen2.5-14B on two other powered datasets (FOLIO $n = 204$, LogiQA $n = 200$) yields $|\Delta| \leq 0.50$\,pp. Even in-context learning with gold FOL examples (SC $= 74.37\%$, $\Delta = +0.50$\,pp, $n = 199$) fails to break the pattern: improving extraction quality through exemplars does not overcome confirmation bias when the model already produces consistent traces. Qwen3-14B (SC $= 84.80\%$) represents a generational capability improvement yet produces $\Delta = -0.49$\,pp ($p > 0.05$).
67	
68	\paragraph{Type C (SC $\leq$ $\sim$40\%): error amplification.} Mistral-7B on ProofWriter depth-5 ($n = 600$, SC $= 39.33\%$) shows $\Delta = -2.83$\,pp ($p = 0.014$): SICA \emph{significantly hurts} performance. Constraints extracted from predominantly incorrect traces encode wrong reasoning as formal rules, and the solver amplifies these errors rather than correcting them.
69	
70	\paragraph{Degenerate cases.} When $C_0 < 5\%$ (QwQ-32B on AIME 2024, Qwen2.5-14B on GSM8K), nearly all traces agree and SICA reduces to SC by construction. These probes confirm the $C_0$ diagnostic (\S\ref{sec:method}).
71	
72	Figure~\ref{fig:regime-scatter} visualizes the regime dependence. The intermediate-SC region is narrow and observed only for Mistral-7B on FOLIO: the upper boundary is sharp (LLaMA-3.1-8B on FOLIO at SC $= 66.18\%$ already shows $\Delta = -4.41$\,pp), and below $\sim$40\% SC, constraints transition from noisy to actively harmful. The oracle rows (bottom of Table~\ref{tab:main_results}) confirm that gold constraints yield $\Delta = +14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter (both $p < 0.001$), establishing that the aggregation mechanism is sound when constraints are discriminative (\S\ref{sec:oracle}).

Type~C (SC $\leq$ 40\%): SICA significantly hurts ($\Delta = -2.83$\,pp, $p = 0.014$).}
78	\label{fig:regime-scatter}
79	\end{figure}

82	\subsection{Oracle Control: The Aggregation Mechanism Is Sound}
83	\label{sec:oracle}
84	
85	Oracle variants replace self-extracted constraints with gold annotations: FOL formulas from FOLIO ($n = 204$) and domain-specific logic (DSL) programs from ProofWriter ($n = 600$). The oracle evaluates gold constraints against each candidate answer via Z3 directly; the scoring function (Eq.~\ref{eq:score}) remains unchanged. This design functions as a causal intervention on constraint quality while holding the aggregation mechanism constant.
86	
87	Oracle-SICA achieves 89.71\% on FOLIO versus 75.49\% for SC ($\Delta = +14.22$\,pp, $p = 2.0 \times 10^{-7}$, McNemar $b = 29$, $c = 0$). Z3 agrees with gold labels on 95.1\% of FOLIO problems (194/204). On ProofWriter, Oracle-SICA reaches 86.67\% versus 75.17\% ($\Delta = +11.50$\,pp, $p = 9.21 \times 10^{-15}$), with Z3 gold agreement of 97.1\% (577/594). Relational subtypes benefit most: RelNeg $+17.86$\,pp and RelNoneg $+13.01$\,pp (Appendix Table~\ref{tab:pw_oracle_subtype}).

89	These results establish two conclusions. First, the MAX-SAT aggregation mechanism is sound: given discriminative constraints, it produces large and highly significant gains. In the intermediate-SC region (SC $\sim$50--55\%), Mistral-7B on FOLIO shows positive directional trends in 2 of 4 seeds. Seed~42 achieves $\Delta = +3.43$\,pp ($p = 0.092$, marginal) and seed~123 shows $\Delta = +2.94$\,pp ($p = 0.070$, marginal); the remaining seeds show null or negative results ($\Delta = 0.00$ and $-0.49$\,pp; see \S\ref{sec:replication}). \paragraph{Type A (SC $\geq$ $\sim$60\%): confirmation bias.} Nine conditions with SC $\geq 63\%$ (combined $N > 2{,}800$) produce no significant positive effects. Most yield $|\Delta| \leq 2.45$\,pp (nonsignificant), but LLaMA-3.1-8B on FOLIO shows $\Delta = -4.41$\,pp ($p = 0.093$, marginal) and Qwen2.5-14B on ProofWriter ($n = 600$, SC $= 75.17\%$) shows a significant negative effect: $\Delta = -2.50$\,pp ($p = 0.011$), indicating that symbolic aggregation can hurt even when the model is accurate. Qwen3-14B (SC $= 84.80\%$) represents a generational capability improvement yet produces $\Delta = -0.49$\,pp ($p > 0.05$).

Constraints extracted from predominantly incorrect traces encode wrong reasoning as formal rules, and the solver amplifies these errors rather than correcting them.

\subsection{Oracle Control: The Aggregation Mechanism Is Sound}
\label{sec:oracle}

Oracle variants replace self-extracted constraints with gold annotations: FOL formulas from FOLIO ($n = 204$) and domain-specific logic (DSL) programs from ProofWriter ($n = 600$). The oracle evaluates gold constraints against each candidate answer via Z3 directly; the scoring function (Eq.~\ref{eq:score}) remains unchanged. This design functions as a causal intervention on constraint quality while holding the aggregation mechanism constant.

Oracle-SICA achieves 89.71\% on FOLIO versus 75.49\% for SC ($\Delta = +14.22$\,pp, $p = 2.0 \times 10^{-7}$, McNemar $b = 29$, $c = 0$). Z3 agrees with gold labels on 95.1\% of FOLIO problems (194/204). On ProofWriter, Oracle-SICA reaches 86.67\% versus 75.17\% ($\Delta = +11.50$\,pp, $p = 9.21 \times 10^{-15}$), with Z3 gold agreement of 97.1\% (577/594). Relational subtypes benefit most: RelNeg $+17.86$\,pp and RelNoneg $+13.01$\,pp (Appendix Table~\ref{tab:pw_oracle_subtype}).

These results establish two conclusions. First, the MAX-SAT aggregation mechanism is sound: given discriminative constraints, it produces large and highly significant gains. Second, the gap between self-extraction and oracle performance quantifies the independence bottleneck. Mistral-7B's best self-extracted result ($+3.43$\,pp) captures only 24.1\% of the FOLIO oracle ceiling ($+14.22$\,pp). The remaining 75.9\% is lost to self-extraction quality. Section~\ref{sec:failure-modes} decomposes this loss into three distinct failure modes.


\subsection{Four-Seed Replication}
\label{sec:replication}

No seed reaches statistical significance at $\alpha = 0.05$; 2 of 4 show marginal positive trends ($p < 0.10$). The mean effect across four seeds is $\Delta = +1.47$\,pp, with effects ranging from $+3.43$ to $-0.49$\,pp. Cross-seed variance is high, confirming that even the most promising condition produces unreliable improvements.

The variance is informative. Seeds~42 and~456 share identical SC baselines (55.88\%) yet produce different SICA outcomes ($+3.43$ vs.\ $0.00$\,pp), indicating that SC level alone does not determine the effect; seed-level constraint quality also matters. Sampling noise at the regime boundary can push individual seeds across the transition, which makes the effect fragile by design rather than by accident. This seed-level sensitivity motivates the entropy decomposition in \S\ref{sec:entropy}, where per-problem trace agreement reveals that the aggregate $\Delta$ is driven entirely by the high-entropy subpopulation: seed~42 achieves $+12.8$\,pp on high-entropy problems while seed~456 shows $-1.3$\,pp on the same partition.

\label{sec:failure-modes}

\paragraph{Type A: confirmation bias (SC $\geq$ $\sim$60\%).} Strong models produce consistent reasoning traces, and constraints extracted from those traces mirror the answer distribution. When most constraints support the same candidate, MAX-SAT excludes few clauses ($|\mathcal{C}^{\setminus}| \approx 0$), the penalty term in Eq.~\ref{eq:score} vanishes, and the scoring function degenerates to weighted vote counting (Eq.~\ref{eq:degenerate}). SICA and SC then produce identical predictions. The ablation in \S\ref{sec:ablation} confirms this empirically: on Qwen2.5-14B (FOLIO + ProofWriter, $n = 804$), MAX-SAT and count-only baselines agree on 803 of 804 predictions.

\paragraph{Type B: non-formalizable domains.} LogiQA problems require pragmatic and contextual reasoning that resists clean FOL formalization. Qwen2.5-14B on LogiQA achieves an extraction rate of 86.4\% (fraction of traces yielding at least one parseable constraint), but the resulting constraints have a contradiction rate of only 0.8\%: extracted formulas rarely conflict across traces, leaving MAX-SAT with no logical tension to exploit. Mistral-7B on LogiQA sits in the same SC range (51.00\%) yet produces $\Delta = +0.50$\,pp ($p = 1.0$); Qwen2.5-14B on the same domain yields $\Delta = -0.50$\,pp ($p = 1.0$).
